title: Deciding the Desired Outcome of Meetings Before They Begin
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that stating a meeting's desired outcome before it starts matters more than having a good agenda, though most organizations skip this step. It reasons that a clear outcome should actually determine the agenda and attendee list, rather than the other way around, using the analogy of buying ingredients without first knowing the dish being cooked. The article lists a range of possible meeting outcomes, from shared understanding to concrete decisions, to illustrate how varied and specific this framing device can be. It closes by noting how rarely this simple practice is actually used despite its outsized impact on meeting effectiveness.
points: Argues stated outcomes should precede and shape the meeting agenda, not follow it
Uses a cooking analogy to explain the logical order of outcome-then-agenda
Lists a range of possible meeting outcomes to show the technique's flexibility
Notes the practice is rare despite being simple and highly effective
quotes: Meetings are the hard labor of the modern organization. They are costly, time-consuming, and essential.
Any meeting without a well-defined agenda suffers the fate of wasteful conversations and continual digression away from what needs to be discussed.
The best leaders always state the desired outcome of the meeting before it begins.
Crafting a meeting agenda without first clearly articulating the desired outcome is akin to buying ingredients for a meal without knowing the dish.
Truth be known, meetings that begin with clearly articulated outcomes are the exception, not the rule, in nearly all organizations.
Sometimes, simplicity is not as obvious as we like to think.
